passage:
Trisha wanted to be a software architect by twenty-nine. She began at the end and listed what the role demanded: designing whole systems, guiding a team and knowing her industry in depth. Then she put each item against a year.

For the first year, she called her theme "core skills." The second year was about owning a module. Each quarter she wrote a pair of concrete, countable goals and reviewed them in a note of a few lines.

Samir, her friend, took a different route. Every time a company offered more pay, he moved. He never stayed long enough to finish a big project or learn a system well. After four years his resume showed many company names, but no direction, and the recruiter who called last spring could not say what he was best at.

Every December, Trisha sat down with her plan and compared results with what she had promised herself. This year she crossed out a goal that no longer fitted, because the market had shifted, and added another that suited her life better since she had a baby coming. Beside each change she wrote why. Anjali, reading over her shoulder, said, "So it's a plan you can bend?" "Yes," said Trisha, "and a record of why I bent it."

qa.q: What did Trisha call her theme for the first year?
How did Samir's career moves differ from Trisha's plan, and what did his resume show after four years?
qa.a: Samir followed whichever company paid most and never stayed long enough to learn deeply, so his resume showed many names but no direction, while Trisha worked backward from architect and assigned skills to years.

qa.q: What was Samir probably feeling when the recruiter could not say what he was best at?
qa.a: He was probably unsettled or embarrassed, as the lack of depth and direction became visible.

qa.q: What did Trisha's December review add to her plan?
qa.a: It let her compare results, drop a goal that no longer fitted, add a new one and record why, so the plan stays useful as life and the market change.

grounding: An approach comparison for a five-year career strategy: working backward from a target role, yearly themes with quarterly goals, chasing the highest salary, and an annual review and replan.
